text:
A: Hello! Hello, Darren, yes? I'm Danuta. Can you hear me okay?
B: Yeah, I can hear you. Alright.
A: Good, good. This is my second one, I'm getting better I think. First one I talk too much. Have you had your tea?
B: Not yet. Probably just a pie and oven chips. Can't be bothered cooking just for me, you know.
B: Sorry, that sounds a bit sad, dunt it.
A: No! Is normal. When my husband is on late, I also eat just bread and cheese standing in the kitchen. Where are you, Darren?
B: Castleford. West Yorkshire. You?
A: Preston. But I'm from Poland, near Rzeszów. Twenty years nearly here. I clean on the wards at the hospital.
B: Oh right. Hard graft, that.
A: Is hard on the knees. After an early shift I come home and I sit and I don't move, my husband has to bring me a brew.
B: Tell me about it. I'm a joiner, I'm kneeling on floors all day, fitting boards and that. Me knees are knackered by about two o'clock.
A: So we are the same! Old knees club.
B: Ha. Yeah. Something like that.
A: I liked your photo. The socks on the radiator, I laughed, sorry. My Tadeusz does exactly this.
B: Oh God, did you see them? I didn't even think. Live on me own, nobody to tell me off.
A: And the photo on the wall, the lady at the seaside, this is your mum?
B: Yeah. Me mam, with me sister's kids. Bridlington, I think. She died three year ago.
A: Oh, I'm sorry, love.
B: Ta. It's alright. I've still got all her stuff in boxes in the back bedroom. Can't sort of face going through it yet. Daft, really.
A: Not daft. Not daft at all. When my father died, my mother kept his coat on the door for, oh, five years. Nobody was allowed to touch.
B: Yeah. That's it, innit. You just leave it.
A: She's eighty-four now, my mother, in Poland. I worry all the time. I go every summer, I come back and I cry on the plane, you know?
B: I'm not surprised. That's a long way to be. Must be hard.
A: I go to the Polish Mass on Sunday, I light a candle for her, it helps me a bit. Maybe silly.
B: No, it's not. I go at Christmas, and on the day she died, I sort of... yeah. I'm not much of a churchgoer, but I believe in something, do you know what I mean.
A: Yes. I know exactly. It's good to have something.
B: Anyway. Sorry, bit heavy for three minutes, that.
A: No, no, I like it. Better than talking about weather! So what you do when you are not working? You like the rugby, I think? I saw a blanket.
B: Cas Tigers, yeah. Rugby league. Lost again Sunday. I were in a mood all Monday.
A: My husband the same with football! If Poland loses, I don't talk to him for one day, is safer.
B: Probably wise, that. I go fishing as well, in summer. Fairburn Ings. Just sit there. Nobody bothers you.
A: That sounds peaceful. You should bring your tea, a nice barm, make a day.
B: Barm? Is that a Lancashire thing?
A: Yes! Bacon barm, from the canteen. I learned it at the hospital, now I can't stop saying—
